name: Sten Sture the Elder
causeOfDeath: Not recorded; he died on the road home from Denmark
restingPlace: Strängnäs Cathedral, after Mariefred and Kärnbo
summary: Regent of Sweden for thirty years without a crown, who beat Christian I of Denmark at the Battle of Brunkeberg in 1471, kept the Kalmar Union's kings out of the country for a quarter of a century with the Swedish throne deliberately left empty, and saw Uppsala University chartered in 1477.
title: Regent of Sweden
roles: Knight and member of the Swedish council

birth.note: Neither year nor place is recorded. Reference works print about 1440; the Svenskt biografiskt lexikon prefers about 1437, which would make him roughly sixty-six rather than sixty-three at his death.

death.circumstance: Died on the journey back from escorting the captive Queen Christina to the Danish border. His chancellor Hemming Gadh concealed the death for days, moving the body in a merchant's sledge wrapped in hides while a servant of similar build rode in the regent's place, until Svante Nilsson's election was secure.

quickFacts.knownFor: Brunkeberg in 1471, and thirty years of regency against the Kalmar Union

imageInfo.caption: Georg von Rosen's history painting of 1864, The Entry of Sten Sture the Elder into Stockholm, in the Nationalmuseum. Painted four centuries after the event, it is Swedish national memory rather than a likeness.
imageInfo.creator: Georg von Rosen
imageInfo.note: Public domain; Nationalmuseum inventory NM 19214. Von Rosen painted the regent's entry into Stockholm as a set piece of the Swedish national-romantic school, with costume and architecture reconstructed from antiquarian study rather than from any fifteenth-century source. No portrait of Sten Sture taken from life is known, so the armoured rider is an invention; the picture is evidence for how the nineteenth century saw him.

overview: Sten Sture the Elder governed Sweden for a little over thirty years and never wore a crown. Elected riksföreståndare — regent, literally the realm's steward — on 1 May 1471, he defeated Christian I of Denmark at the Battle of Brunkeberg outside Stockholm five months later, and then kept the Kalmar Union's kings out of the country for twenty-five years with the Swedish throne deliberately left empty.

His power rested on castles, on the mining and farming commons of the Dalarna country, and on a willingness to summon them against his own aristocracy. That is what the Swedish council finally would not tolerate: it declared him deposed in March 1497 and called in King Hans of Denmark, to whom he submitted that October. The magnates changed their minds, elected him regent again in November 1501, and he died at Jönköping on 14 December 1503 with his death concealed by his chancellor for long enough to arrange the succession.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Sten Sture the Elder governed Sweden for a little over thirty years and never wore a crown. Elected riksföreståndare — regent, literally the realm's steward — on 1 May 1471, he defeated Christian I of Denmark at the Battle of Brunkeberg outside Stockholm five months later, and then kept the Kalmar Union's kings out of the country for twenty-five years with the Swedish throne deliberately left empty.

His power rested on castles, on the mining and farming commons of the Dalarna country, and on a willingness to summon them against his own aristocracy. That is what the Swedish council finally would not tolerate: it declared him deposed in March 1497 and called in King Hans of Denmark, to whom he submitted that October. The magnates changed their minds, elected him regent again in November 1501, and he died at Jönköping on 14 December 1503 with his death concealed by his chancellor for long enough to arrange the succession.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: He was born about 1440 — the Svenskt biografiskt lexikon prefers about 1437 — and no source gives the place. His father, Gustav Anundsson Sture, sat on the council of the realm and died in 1444, when the boy was small; his mother was Birgitta Stensdotter of the Bielke family, and she was the half-sister of Karl Knutsson Bonde, who ruled Sweden three separate times as Charles VIII of Sweden. Sten was brought up by his mother and her second husband, Gustav Karlsson, at Kalmar and at the family seat of Ekholmen in Uppland.

That kinship was the making of him, but so was a marriage. Knighted in 1462 and on the council by 1466, he married Ingeborg Åkesdotter of the Tott family in the latter year, which placed him inside the network of the Axelsson brothers — a private Baltic interest holding castles and islands across Denmark, Sweden and Finland, and for a generation the most formidable power bloc in the north that was not a crown.

He learned the war young. In 1464 he fought in Bishop Kettil Karlsson Vasa's rising against Christian I and won an engagement at Haraker in Västmanland. Six years later, dying in May 1470, Karl Knutsson handed him his castles and towns, Stockholm among them. Sweden's next head of state was chosen by a king's deathbed disposition of real property, which says a good deal about how the kingdom actually worked.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: The first difficulty with Sten Sture's character is that he wrote a good deal of it himself. The Sturekrönikan — the closing section of the Stora rimkrönikan, covering 1452 to 1496 — is really two chronicles bound together, and the first, running to 1487, was in all probability commissioned by Sten Sture. The standard heroic narrative of his rise is therefore his own campaign literature in rhyme. The second part was written about a decade later on Archbishop Jakob Ulvsson's initiative, and it attacks him hard and argues that he should be removed from the regency. One chronicle, two patrons, two Sten Stures; where they agree is where the evidence is firmest.

What both halves show, from opposite sides, is the method that defined him. He went over the heads of the council to the commons. He summoned peasants and miners to assemblies, used the Dalarna levies as an army and as an argument, and made himself a man the aristocracy could not remove without asking the country first. His supporters called that the realm's liberty; the magnates called it demagoguery and a standing threat to their own standing, and in 1497 they acted on the second reading.

Modern scholarship has stripped a good deal of varnish off. Sven Ulric Palme's study of 1950 set aside the national hero and described a formidable accumulator: a financier, a land speculator and an exporter who gathered fiefs, mines and money on a scale no Swedish magnate had managed, and who understood as well as anyone in Europe what a commissioned chronicle, a votive monument and an annual procession were for. Palme's sharpest point is that the lines of Sten Sture's posthumous portrait were drawn in his own lifetime, and that historians from Johannes Magnus onward simply followed them. He was a genuinely skilled politician, and one of his skills was arranging how he would be remembered.

contentSections.title: Elected regent, 1470–71
paragraphs: Charles VIII of Sweden died on 15 May 1470, the last king the Swedes had elected for themselves, and Sten took possession of the castles left to him. He was elected riksföreståndare on 1 May 1471, with the Axelsson brothers' backing, and the choice was confirmed at an assembly at Arboga that May which nobles, burghers and peasants attended — the estates machinery improvised in Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson's generation, now used to install a head of state.

The office needs stating precisely, because it is easy to mistake for something else. A riksföreståndare was not a regent for an absent or infant king in the ordinary European sense, and certainly not a monarch. Sweden simply had no king: the union crown belonged in law to Christian I of Denmark, the Swedes declined to give it to him, and rather than elect a rival they left the throne vacant and appointed a steward to exercise royal government. It was a constitutional improvisation, and it lasted, with interruptions, for half a century.
It also had to be defended within months. Christian I was not prepared to be legislated out of a kingdom, and in the autumn of 1471 he came to Stockholm with a fleet and an army to take it back.

contentSections.title: Brunkeberg, 1471
paragraphs: Christian encamped on the Brunkeberg ridge immediately north of Stockholm, blocking the landward approach while Sten gathered levies in the country behind him. Modern estimates put the Danish force at around six thousand, roughly half of it German mercenaries, and the Swedish at up to ten thousand, most of them Dalarna and Uppland levies rather than professional soldiers; these are estimates from later reconstruction rather than counts, and the numbers matter less than the shape of the day.

On 10 October 1471 Sten attacked the ridge from the west and held Christian's front. Nils Sture brought a second force out of the woods on the north-east flank, and Knut Posse led the Stockholm burghers out of the city and over the bridge into the Danish rear. Christian took a handgun shot in the face that cost him several teeth. Caught between the sortie and the flank attack, part of his army was cut off and the rest broke toward the ships. The Battle of Brunkeberg was the most complete victory Sweden won in the union century.

What it bought was time, which is what he wanted. Christian never recovered the kingdom, Sten's election stopped being provisional, and the Danish claim was not pressed in arms again for a generation. He was also careful about what the victory should mean: he had put his army under the protection of Saint George before the battle, and he paid for the consequences of that vow in oak, gold and elk antler eighteen years later.

contentSections.title: Uppsala University and the regent's peace
paragraphs: The decision to found a studium generale at Uppsala was taken at a meeting at Strängnäs in 1477, on the initiative of Archbishop Jakob Ulvsson and with the regent's backing. Sixtus IV's bull of 27 February 1477 granted the new university the privileges of Bologna — the four faculties of theology, law, medicine and philosophy, the right to confer degrees up to the doctorate, and the archbishop of Uppsala as its chancellor — and lectures began on 7 October that year.

It mattered because of what it replaced. Swedish clerks and administrators had until then gone abroad for their degrees, to Paris, Prague, Leipzig and Rostock, and a realm arguing that it could govern itself without a king had an obvious interest in training its own men at home. The first Swedish university was in that sense a political statement as much as a scholarly one. It was also fragile: teaching stopped in 1515 and the university did not properly revive until the 1590s.

Sten Sture's personal share in it is easier to assert than to document, and the two main sources pull in opposite directions in the usual way. The Sture chronicle is keen to give him the credit; the papal bull answers the archbishop, whose project it plainly was. What can be said without strain is that the foundation happened under his government, with his support, in the years when his authority was least contested.

contentSections.title: The council turns, 1497
paragraphs: The Kalmar Recess of 1483 acknowledged Hans of Denmark as king of Sweden, and Sten spent the next fourteen years never quite refusing to admit him. He broke the last of his old patrons in 1487, manoeuvring Ivar Axelsson Tott out of his castles and out of the kingdom. By the 1490s he had no rivals left in Sweden and correspondingly few friends on the council.

The break came out of Finland. King Hans encouraged Ivan III of Moscow against the Swedes, Russian forces came into Finland in 1495, and Knut Posse held the castle of Viborg through a Russian assault that Swedish tradition turned into a miracle story. Sten quarrelled with Svante Nilsson over the conduct of the campaign; Svante went home, made common cause with Archbishop Ulvsson, and carried the council with him. In March 1497 the riksråd declared Sten deposed, citing his conduct in Finland and his refusal to obey it. He declined to surrender his castles.

It was settled by force and then by bargain. On 28 September 1497 Danish troops cut up a Dalecarlian army at Rotebro north of Stockholm, and on 6 October Sten met King Hans in person and gave up the government. He kept a great deal: fiefs including Finland and Nyköping castle, and the office of court master at Hans's Swedish coronation. A man who had ruled for twenty-six years walked away from it into the winner's household, which is not the behaviour of the patriot of the paintings and is very much the behaviour of the politician Palme described.

contentSections.title: Return and death
paragraphs: The magnates who had recalled Hans discovered what the Swedes usually discovered about union kings, and on 1 August 1501 they conspired against him. Sten was elected regent a second time on 12 November 1501. Hemming Gadh's diplomacy and a long blockade brought in the Tre Kronor castle at Stockholm in the spring of 1502, when Queen Christina surrendered it after holding out through the winter, and by the end of that year Sten held every part of Sweden except Kalmar and Öland.

He died at Jönköping on 14 December 1503, on the road back from escorting Queen Christina to the Danish border. What happened next is the most characteristic episode in his story, and he had no part in it: Hemming Gadh kept the death secret, loaded the body into a merchant's sledge wrapped in hides, and set a servant of similar build in the regent's saddle, so that the succession could be arranged before anyone in Denmark or on the council learned that Sweden had no head of state. Svante Nilsson — the man whose quarrel had helped bring him down in 1497 — was elected in his place.

The body travelled as far after death as the regency did. It was laid for a short time in the base of the Saint George group in Storkyrkan, then taken in 1504 to the Charterhouse at Mariefred which he had founded; after the house was dissolved the coffin went to Kärnbo church, and in 1576 to Strängnäs Cathedral, where Gustav III put him into a green marble sarcophagus in 1774.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: The monument he commissioned outlasted the politics. Bernt Notke's Saint George and the Dragon, inaugurated in Storkyrkan on New Year's Eve 1489, is the thank-offering for Brunkeberg: oak, metal, leather, real hair and elk antlers for the dragon's spikes, standing about six metres with its plinth, with the saint's plume in blue and yellow. For decades afterwards it was carried in procession to the battlefield every 10 October. It is the finest late-medieval sculpture in Sweden and it is also a piece of political argument, which is the combination Sten Sture was best at.

The constitutional legacy is larger. Between 1470 and 1520 Sweden worked out a way of being a kingdom without a king — an elected steward exercising royal government, answerable to a council he usually fought and to assemblies of estates he usually summoned over the council's head. Sten Sture the Elder made that arrangement stick for thirty years, his successors Svante Nilsson and Sten Sture the Younger carried it to 1520, and Gustav Vasa's secession of 1523 was built on the template. Uppsala, chartered under him, is the other institution that survived.

What has not survived scrutiny is the version in the paintings. Georg von Rosen's entry into Stockholm of 1864 belongs to a nineteenth century that wanted a national liberator, and Palme's reassessment of 1950 was aimed squarely at it. The man in the sources is harder, richer and more interesting than the man on the canvas: an operator who fought a twenty-five-year holding action against a union crown, made a fortune while doing it, lost everything to his own council in a season, and took it all back four years later.

keyAchievements.title: Won the Battle of Brunkeberg, 1471
keyAchievements.description: The three-pronged attack on the ridge north of Stockholm on 10 October broke Christian I's army and wounded the king, ending the Danish attempt to retake Sweden by force.

keyAchievements.title: Governed Sweden for thirty years without a crown
keyAchievements.description: Elected riksföreståndare on 1 May 1471 and again on 12 November 1501, he exercised royal government with the Swedish throne deliberately left vacant.

keyAchievements.title: Uppsala University chartered under his government
keyAchievements.description: Sixtus IV's bull of 27 February 1477 gave Sweden its first university the privileges of Bologna; lectures began that October.

keyAchievements.title: Commissioned Notke's Saint George and the Dragon
keyAchievements.description: The great Storkyrkan group of 1489 was his thank-offering for Brunkeberg, and was carried to the battlefield each year on the anniversary.

timeline.title: Marriage into the Tott interest
timeline.description: His marriage to Ingeborg Åkesdotter placed him inside the Axelsson brothers' network of castles and lordships across the Baltic.

timeline.title: Charles VIII dies and leaves him the castles
timeline.description: The last king the Swedes elected for themselves disposed of Stockholm and his other strongholds to Sten on his deathbed.

timeline.title: Elected regent of the realm
timeline.description: Chosen riksföreståndare with the Axelssons' support and confirmed at an Arboga assembly attended by nobles, burghers and peasants.

timeline.title: Victory at the Battle of Brunkeberg
timeline.description: Christian I is wounded and his army broken between Sten's frontal attack, Nils Sture's flanking force and Knut Posse's sortie from Stockholm.

timeline.title: Uppsala University chartered
timeline.description: Sixtus IV's bull grants Sweden's first university the privileges of Bologna; teaching begins on 7 October.

timeline.title: The Kalmar Recess names Hans king
timeline.description: Sweden formally acknowledges Hans of Denmark as its king, and Sten spends the next fourteen years never quite letting him take possession.

timeline.title: Notke's Saint George inaugurated
timeline.description: The thank-offering for Brunkeberg is set up in Storkyrkan on New Year's Eve and afterwards carried to the battlefield each anniversary.

timeline.title: The council deposes him
timeline.description: The riksråd declares the regency forfeit over his conduct of the Finnish war and his disobedience, and recalls King Hans.

timeline.title: Submission to King Hans
timeline.description: After a Dalecarlian army is beaten at Rotebro, Sten surrenders the government in person in exchange for Finland, Nyköping and a court office.

timeline.title: Elected regent a second time
timeline.description: The magnates turn on Hans, and Sten returns to the regency; Stockholm castle falls back into Swedish hands the following spring.

timeline.title: Death at Jönköping
timeline.description: He dies returning from the Danish border, and Hemming Gadh hides the death until Svante Nilsson's election is arranged.

sectionImages.alt: Painted and gilded wooden sculpture of a mounted knight in armour striking down a spiked dragon, inside a brick-vaulted church.
sectionImages.caption: Bernt Notke's Saint George and the Dragon in Storkyrkan, Stockholm, carved in oak with elk antler and inaugurated on New Year's Eve 1489. Sten Sture commissioned it as his thank-offering for Brunkeberg.
sectionImages.creator: Sculptor Bernt Notke; photograph by Dennis G. Jarvis
sectionImages.note: CC BY-SA 2.0. The group stands about six metres tall with its plinth and is built of oak with metal, leather, human hair and elk antlers for the dragon's spikes; the saint's plume is blue and yellow. It depicts Saint George rather than Sten Sture, but it was made to commemorate his victory, and his body lay briefly in its base after his death.

succession.note: Sten Sture was never king, and the boxes show the headship of the realm rather than a crown. Sweden left the throne vacant from 1470: the regent exercised royal government on the council's authority.

predecessor.note: His mother's half-brother and the last king the Swedes elected for themselves; on his death in May 1470 the throne was left empty and Sten took his castles.

successor.note: Elected regent in January 1504, half a century past IronCodex's 1453 cutoff. King Hans of Denmark held the Swedish crown in person between Sten's two terms, from 1497 to 1501.
